notes:
I've grouped these notes by verse. Each point gives its source page. Some gaps:

- **Not found:** anything on newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org, netbible.org notes, bibleodyssey.org, or prosperity / word-of-faith / hyper-grace sites. So the "other views" below are only patristic and Vulgate readings quoted inside the older commentaries.
- **Pentecostal, Lutheran and Methodist:** I found no teachers from these traditions who say they speak for them.
- **Tradition labels:** I only name a tradition where the page itself labels it.
- **Pulpit Commentary:** the full chapter page cut off at v. 7. For vv. 8–18 I used shorter search excerpts.

---

**Overview**
- Guzik (Enduring Word) reads the chapter as Solomon urging people to enjoy life because death is coming. On his reading the Preacher speaks from a bleak "under the sun" view, where everyone shares the same end whatever their righteousness.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-9/

**v. 1**
- Guzik says the "under the sun" outlook leaves out eternity. Creation shows that God exists, but it does not clearly show that God loves us.  His fix is to measure God's love by the cross, not by what happens to us.  He also thinks the Preacher has let belief in God's sovereignty slide into fatalism.  — https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/ecclesiastes/ecclesiastes-9.cfm
- Pulpit Commentary: "love or hatred" means God's favour or displeasure. You can't read God's view of a person from what happens to them, and we shouldn't judge like Job's friends.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/9.htm
- Ellicott (labelled "Arminian… Anglican" on StudyLight) reads it differently: because of v. 6, it means a person's own love or hatred, whose targets he can't know in advance.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ecclesiastes/9-1.html
- Gill gives an "evangelical" reading: the righteous here are those made righteous by Christ's obedience, held safe in God's hand.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ecclesiastes/9-1.html
- **Other views (Catholic and patristic):** Pulpit notes that the Vulgate takes the verse as "man does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred." It also quotes St Gregory: you can't foresee your own end, or how strictly God weighs your good deeds. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/9.htm

**v. 2**
- Pulpit lists five contrasting pairs. It reads the last pair as the careless or false swearer against the person who treats an oath as holy. It also gives Plumptre's other view, that the one who swears is doing his religious duty properly. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/9.htm
- Guzik says this is how things *seemed* to Solomon from his "under the sun" premise.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-9/

**v. 3**
- Pulpit: the "one event" is death. Because fate looks random, people sin recklessly. "Madness" means behaviour against wisdom and reason.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/9.htm
- Guzik: the Preacher states the common fate but "does not like it."  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-9/

**v. 4**
- Pulpit: in that culture the dog was despised and the lion was the noblest beast. So the proverb means the lowest living thing beats the greatest dead one.  It sees no real clash with 4:2 or 7:1. Here life is valued as a chance for enjoyment, while there death is welcomed as an end to misery.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/9.htm
- Ellicott notes a variant in the Hebrew text: "chosen" instead of "joined," which can be read as "who is excepted?"  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/9.htm
- Guzik: if death ends everything, only this life matters, and so nothing really matters.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-9/

**vv. 5–6 (where readers disagree most: what happens to the dead)**
- Guzik: Solomon puts forward, poetically, the belief that existence and consciousness end at death. Guzik frames this as the "under the sun" premise, not as final truth.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-9/
- Barnes (labelled "Presbyterian · Calvinism" on StudyLight): the dead are unconscious *as far as this life goes*. Solomon describes what he sees, not what he believes about the soul.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/9-5.htm
- Gill: the righteous dead know far more than they did in life, and the wicked dead feel hell's torments. The verse refers only to bodily senses and earthly matters. He adds that for this reason the dead should not be prayed to as go-betweens with God. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/9-5.htm
- Constable: "know nothing" doesn't mean the dead feel nothing. Later revelation (Luke 16) shows they are aware. In context it means they can't enjoy life as the living do.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ecclesiastes/9-5.html
- Clarke: their time of testing (probation) is over, so there is no further reward or punishment for life on earth.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ecclesiastes/9-5.html
- **Groups outside mainstream Protestantism:** Coffman says Seventh-day Adventists use this verse to argue that no soul is conscious after death. He calls this a false doctrine. Note that the quotation he gives is actually from a Watchtower (Jehovah's Witness) publication.  Chuck Smith (labelled "Calvary Chapel") says people who teach the soul is annihilated cite this verse, though Ecclesiastes deals with human reason apart from God.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ecclesiastes/9-5.html
- A Bible Hub Q&A article: "under the sun" means the earthly view. Sheol means being absent from earthly life, not necessarily having no consciousness at all.  — https://biblehub.com/q/how_does_ecclesiastes_9_5_fit_with_an_active_afterlife.htm
- Pulpit: there is a wordplay in Hebrew between "memory" (zeker) and "reward" (sakar).  On v. 6, it says the gloomy view matches the Old Testament, and that Christ "brought life and immortality to light." The writer still believes the soul goes on existing. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/9.htm

**v. 7 (what "God has approved your works" means)**
- Pulpit: "works" means the eating and drinking themselves, not moral deeds that earn blessings.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/9.htm
- Benson: God accepts the services of the truly godly and lets them enjoy his blessings.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/9-7.htm
- Geneva Study Bible note, more suspicious: people flatter themselves that they are in God's favour because they have plenty.  — same URL
- Guzik hears both fatalism and wishful thinking: perhaps "God accepts your works – *I hope*."  — https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/ecclesiastes/ecclesiastes-9.cfm
- Ellicott: earthly enjoyment is to be received as a gift of God's favour.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/9.htm
- **Other views (Catholic Bible):** the Douay-Rheims translates it "because thy works please God."  — https://biblehub.com/ecclesiastes/9-7.htm

**v. 8**
- Pulpit: white clothes stood for joy and purity.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/9.htm
- Eaton, quoted by Guzik: white clothes and oil make life more comfortable in a hot climate. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-9/

**v. 9**
- Pulpit: here the Preacher balances his harsh words about women in 7:26 by praising a loving wife.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/9-9.htm
- Gill: "portion" also hints that we should seek another portion in the life to come.  — same URL
- Eaton, quoted by Guzik: marriage calls for affection and a lifelong effort to enjoy life together. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-9/

**v. 10**
- Guzik applies the verse to serving God now. He quotes Spurgeon: no one ever served God "by doing things tomorrow."  — https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/ecclesiastes/ecclesiastes-9.cfm
- Pulpit links the verse to John 9:4 ("the night cometh, when no man can work") and 2 Corinthians 6:2. The dead can no longer work or plan.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ecclesiastes/9.htm
- Pulpit Homiletics: work for the world's good has to be done in this short life.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/ecclesiastes/9.htm

**v. 11**
- Guzik: the Preacher again struggles with fatalism. Having said God governs everything, he now wonders whether it is all time and chance.  — https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/ecclesiastes/ecclesiastes-9.cfm
- Gill: these "times" seem random to people but are fixed by God.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/9-11.htm
- Ellicott cross-references Romans 9:16. The word "chance" appears elsewhere only in 1 Kings 5:4.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/9.htm

**v. 12**
- Guzik: from the "under the sun" view, people seem more at the mercy of time and chance than of a loving God.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-9/
- Ellicott cross-references Proverbs 7:23, Ezekiel 12:13 and Hosea 7:12.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/9.htm

**vv. 13–15**
- Ellicott: attempts to find a real historical event behind the story are "idle." It closely resembles the wise woman who saved Abel-beth-maacah in 2 Samuel 20.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/9.htm
- Guzik: if being remembered is the only lasting meaning, even that was taken from him. But people forget and God never does (Malachi 3:16; Luke 10:20).  — https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/ecclesiastes/ecclesiastes-9.cfm
- Pulpit Homiletics compares it to Jesus rejected as "the carpenter's son."  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/ecclesiastes/9.htm

**vv. 16–17**
- Guzik: wisdom is better than strength even when it goes unappreciated, so it should be heard above fools' shouting.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-9/

**v. 18**
- Guzik: it is easier to destroy than to build. He quotes Deane (Pulpit Commentary) giving examples: Adam, Achan and Rehoboam.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-9/
- Pulpit Homiletics: one person's bad example can lead many astray.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/ecclesiastes/9.htm
